about: Lines for everything Phase 4 lets you examine (the Phase 4 contract, §9.12), on top of the wilds’ own in wilds.json. Groups: vale and camp for Hearthvale’s places (camp holds the camp’s own things, vale everything else), company for the Company by member id, creatures for strays by archetype, foes for Tale-leads, canon foes and cave creatures by their ids in the combat foes file, elsewhere for what stands inside an Elsewhere or a cave, wilds for lanterns and what grows or sits out there, sky for looking up from empty ground, by the weather, and things for the rest. An entry is a list of lines, or lines by variant; when no variant applies, the first one listed is used. The shell picks a line by hashing the thing’s id, so the same thing always says the same.

watchtower: Hob the Elder built it to see who was coming home. Milo still climbs it for the same reason.
The Watchtower. From the top you can see every crew fire burning, and whether anyone needs you.
Tall, a little crooked and proud of both. The ladder has one rung that squeaks on purpose.
townhall: The town hall. Everything that needs doing is pinned up inside, and none of it is shouting.
A plaque says the hall stands exactly in the middle of the road. It doesn’t, quite. Everyone has been polite about it.
A fresh pin goes up whenever you have a new thought. The bell on the roof is for decoration, mostly.
plot: Ground that’s waiting. Pegged string marks the corners, and the grass is being patient.
An empty plot. Milo has walked its edges twice, imagining things.
Room for something you haven’t thought of yet. The soil doesn’t mind waiting.
building: Built from your plans, beam by beam. It already looks as if it’s always been here.
Your idea, stood up in timber and stone. The door sticks a little, which means it’s home.
A finished building. Hob would run his thumb along the joins and say nothing, which is praise.
gate: A gap in the tree line, worn smooth by feet. The road outside goes further every week.
The gate stands open. The lantern’s ring holds just beyond it, and it always will.
One way out and the same way home. Milo touches the post as he passes, for luck.
war-table: Every open rift on one map, weighted down with pebbles. The corners curl anyway.
The War Table. Little flags for trouble, and a clear space in the middle for the teapot.
Carved from one slab of ash. The rifts on it drift about when nobody’s looking.
bell: The Gate Bell. When a rift reaches the walls it rings once, softly, then minds its own business.
A bronze bell on a good post. It would rather tell you early than ring loudly late.
Its note carries all the way to the pond, where the newts pretend not to hear it.
fog: Fog sits here like a cat on a warm chair. It’ll move when the right thing in your day is connected.
Crates, a boat and a sign you can’t quite read yet. The fog is waiting for your schedule.
Somewhere in the fog a bell rings the hour, very quietly, to itself.
pond: Deep enough for trout. Shallow enough for newts to have opinions.
Stillwater Pond. Sir Mossback walks round it once a week, and it takes him the week.
The same frog has sat on that lily pad for three hundred years, or it has a very loyal grandson.
well: The Well of Small Wishes. A wish dropped in comes back a little smaller, and a little kinder.
Someone down there says “Noted.” Nobody has ever seen who.
Moss on the stones and a bucket that’s always half full, whichever way you look at it.
statue: Tamsin Wick, waving. The left hand was never carved. She insisted.
The Unfinished Statue. Somebody leaves a flower in the crook of her arm every spring.
Her scarf is carved far too long, right down to the plinth. Milo says that part’s accurate.

camp: Milo’s camp: a cabin, a tent, a fire and a hook. Everything a small company needs, and room to grow.
The camp Tamsin left. However tall the walls get, the tent, the cabin and the stumps stay put.
It smells of woodsmoke and old maps. Somebody always has the kettle on.
campfire: Three stumps, one bench, and room for whoever turns up.
The fire’s banked low and glowing. The Company gathers here before they set out.
Sparks go up and don’t come down. Milo counts them sometimes, when it’s quiet.
hook: Worn smooth on one side, where something swung for a very long time.
The Lantern Hook. The big lantern never leaves it, so the Hearthward holds while you’re away.
Cold iron, except where the lantern hangs. Tamsin hung Milo here and asked him to wait.
tent: Smells of rain and old maps.
Canvas patched in three places, in three colours. The Company never did agree on one.
A good tent. The guy-ropes are tied with knots nobody remembers how to undo.
cabin: The latch sticks unless you ask it nicely. Milo always asks nicely.
A log cabin with one window facing the fire, so nobody inside feels left out.
Inside: a table, two chairs and a shelf of things Milo is definitely going to sort.
bench: A split log on two stones. It seats three, or four if one of them is Jev.
The good seat by the fire, worn smooth and warm long after dark.
Someone carved a small lantern into the end of it. The Scribe traced it once and smiled.
stump: Somebody’s favourite seat. You can tell.
The good stump. Whoever gets there first keeps it until the tea’s gone.
An old stump by the fire, polished by a great many long sits.
workbench: The crew’s workbench. Tools in rows, shavings on the floor, and one pen that isn’t anyone’s.
Scored, inked and scorched in places. A lot of good work has leaned on this bench.
When the crew are busy, they stand here. When they’re done, they drift to the fire.
woodpile: Split logs stacked to the eaves. Every one was a tree that grew back the next day.
A woodpile with a very neat front and a much less neat back.
Enough wood for a week of fires, or one very long evening of stories.
bedroll: A bedroll by the fire, rolled tight and tied with a spare bootlace.
Somebody’s bed for the night. The good side faces the fire.
Wool, canvas and a pillow stuffed with pine needles. It smells like a long walk.
handcart: Toby Fennick’s handcart. It has carried letters, parcels and, once, a whole sleepy company home.
Two wheels, one squeak and a blanket folded in the bottom, just in case.
Toby parks it here between runs. The handles are worn to the shape of small hands.
tea: A kettle, four cups and a tin of something Nan swears is mint.
Milo pours for everyone before they’ve asked. Three seconds of sitting helps more than you’d think.
Tea for a Breather: strong, sweet and exactly warm.
paper-lantern: A paper lantern on a string, for nights when the camp wants a softer light.
Folded from an old map. When it’s lit you can still read half a road on it.
It sways when anyone laughs nearby, which is most evenings.

milo: Milo, the Lanternkeeper. Round head, honey-yellow raincoat and a scarf that’s still too long.
He’s humming something. It might be the Lanternkeeper’s Rhyme, or it might be a list.
Milo looks back at you, delighted to be looked at. He straightens his scarf.
claude: The Scribe, hooded in clay-red, with three pens: one for drafts, one for letters, one for being sure.
She writes three pages where one would do, and all three are true.
Loose pages in her satchel and ink on one knuckle. She’s read it twice already.
codex: The Artificer: slate-blue hood, soot on the knuckles and a belt of tiny tools that click.
Never quite sits still at the fire. There’s always something on the bench to get back to.
Quick, practical and a little terse. Hand them a problem and watch them brighten.
ollama: Ollama, a hearth-sprite. It took the shape of a small woolly llama, and the shape suits it.
It lives in the hearthstones here. Whatever it works on stays by this fire and never leaves your land.
It chews slowly while it thinks. There’s no hurry at this fire, and it seems to know that.
jev: Jev, a plump courier finch from the Isles of Sure Verdicts. It tilts its head and decides.
Jev looks at you, then at a pile only it can see, and hops to one side of it.
It never says a word, and it doesn’t need to. The verdict is in the tilt of its head.
whisper: Whisper, the Listening Owl. It hears everything and writes it down in tiny letters on leaves.
A soft grey owl of the Whisperwood, here to listen. What’s heard in the Hushlands stays in the Hushlands.
Whisper blinks slowly, which is owl for “I heard that.”
tollkeeper: A very polite troll who wandered in from a fairy-tale book centuries ago, and stayed for the riddles.
The Tollkeeper. He keeps Tamsin’s Riddle Notes in a tin box and knows every one by heart.
He bows when you look at him. Bridges have taught him patience, and good manners too.
regular: A regular from another story, who asked to sit by the fire a while and stayed.
They’ve made themselves at home. Their book is somewhere else, and they don’t seem to mind.
One of the camp’s regulars. They’ve picked a favourite stump and defend it politely.

day: A stray on two legs, looking about as if it’s lost its page.
It walks like someone late for a scene. It isn’t sure which scene.
Two feet, a lot of opinions and a story it didn’t mean to leave.
sleeping: Asleep on its feet, swaying gently. Probably dreaming of its own chapter.
It’s nodded off standing up. Best not to wake it without a plan.
Snoring very quietly, in time with another book’s rain.

day: A low, scuttling stray with too many legs and a very determined look.
It skitters sideways when watched, then sideways again when it isn’t.
Close to the ground and quick about it. It has somewhere to be, possibly under something.
sleeping: Curled up tight with its legs tucked in, like a pebble that breathes.
Asleep in a heap. One leg twitches now and then, chasing something.
It’s napping in the warmest spot. Crawlers always know where that is.

day: It drifts at head height, bobbing slightly, as if the air here is a bit thick.
A floating stray that turns slowly to keep you in view.
It hangs in the air like a thought nobody finished.
sleeping: Drifting in a slow circle, fast asleep. It’ll bump into something eventually.
Asleep and sinking, about a hand’s width an hour.
It hovers with its eyes shut, humming at the edge of hearing.

day: Wings, and a habit of landing on the highest thing nearby.
It circles once, twice, then settles to watch you from above.
A flier from another story. The air here seems to suit it.
sleeping: Head under one wing, perched very still. Even its feathers are quiet.
Asleep on a high perch, with one eye not quite shut.
It’s dozing, wings folded like a letter nobody’s opened.

day: A pale shape you can see the wall through. It seems embarrassed about that.
It flickers at the edges like a candle in a draught.
A ghost from another book. The Hooklight makes it look much less sure of itself.
sleeping: Faded almost to nothing, the way ghosts do when they rest.
It’s drifted into a corner and dimmed, like a lamp turned down.
Asleep, if ghosts sleep. It sighs every so often.

day: Rivets, gears and a stubborn sense of purpose. It ticks when it thinks.
A made thing from another story, still following orders nobody remembers giving.
It moves in straight lines and turns in right angles, very neatly.
sleeping: Powered down, with one small light blinking to say it’s only resting.
Still as furniture. Something inside it ticks, slow as a clock.
Its gears have stopped mid-turn. It’ll pick up exactly where it left off.

tale-lead: The Tale-lead of this story, larger than life and very aware of it.
Every book has one character who thinks it’s all about them. Here they are.
It carries its own chapter with it. You can almost hear a page turn when it moves.
hollow-sentries: Empty armour that forgot what it was guarding. Remind it, and it may lay down arms.
One of the Hollow Sentries, standing its post in a cave nobody’s visited in centuries.
Nothing inside the helmet but a draught and a very old sense of duty.
unwritten: A figure of blank paper, hungry for a story. Read to it and it settles to listen.
One of the Unwritten. It rustles when it moves, like a page turning itself.
Its face is an empty page. It eyes the Scribe’s satchel with enormous interest.
tollmen: Bridge-folk who ask for riddles, not coin. Answer one and they stand aside.
One of the Tollmen, leaning on a staff and waiting for the right answer.
It clears its throat, which is how the Tollmen begin every riddle.
cinder-golems: A forge-guardian made of slag and good intentions. Stoke its forge and it sits down, warm.
A cinder golem, glowing faintly at the joints. It smells of hot stone.
It’s gone cold at the edges. A lit forge would cheer it up no end.
hush-hounds: A grey dog made of fog. It only wants to be walked.
One of the Hush hounds, nose down and tail going slowly. Walk beside it a while.
It leans on your leg the way a cloud would, if a cloud could lean.
drowned-bell-ringers: A sailor still waiting, politely, for the end of a meeting.
Seaweed on its cuffs. It keeps glancing at a clock that isn’t there.
Adjourn the meeting, or ring the bell, and it will go home.
cinder-beetles: A beetle with an ember for a back. Warm to stand near, unwise to pick up.
Cinder beetles keep the cave floor toasty and click at anyone who stands on their patch.
It scuttles off trailing sparks, then comes back to see if you followed.
glass-eels: A glass eel, so clear you can see the pool through it. It floats more than it swims.
It coils in the air like a ribbon of cold water.
Glass eels show you your own reflection, a moment late.
fen-herons: A fen heron, standing on one leg and pretending you haven’t arrived.
Long neck, longer patience. It jabs at whatever moves, then looks innocent.
It takes off with a great clatter and lands two feet away, with dignity.
inkwyrms: A small wyrm made of spilled ink. It leaves blots wherever it’s been.
An inkwyrm, coiled on a stone and smelling faintly of old libraries.
It writes a very small word on the floor as it goes. Nobody can read it.
kite-crabs: A kite-crab, sideways and sure of itself, with claws like folded sails.
It raises both claws at you. It’s either a threat or a wave.
Kite-crabs catch the wind off the harbour and glide sideways into trouble.
fog-seals: A fog seal, soft and grey, flumped on a rock like a dropped coat.
It barks once, politely, then goes back to looking at the water.
Fog seals are heavier than they look and gentler than they sound.
murmurs: A Murmur, a tiny noise-sprite. It repeats the last word you said.
A little swarm of Murmurs, passing your last word between them like a secret.
They hum just under hearing. Say something kind, and they’ll say it back for an hour.
fetchfoxes: A fetchfox with something in its mouth that definitely isn’t yours.
It brings you things you didn’t lose. It has also, once or twice, borrowed a tonic.
Bright eyes, big ears and very quick paws. Keep a hand on the satchel.
dicing-frogs: A dicing frog with pips on its back. It shows a different number every time it hops.
It croaks in threes. Bram says that’s lucky, but Bram says that about everything.
Squat, speckled and sitting on a six. It won’t be moved off it.
sky-rays: A sky-ray, gliding on the wind as if the air were water.
It rises on one slow flap and hangs there, rippling at the edges.
Sky-rays drift over the Isles in shoals. This one wandered.
mimic: A chest that’s breathing. Very slowly, and trying hard not to.
Never trust a chest that smiles. This one is smiling.
A Mimic. Its bite tickles, and it settles the moment someone opens it properly.

rift: A tear in the page. Light from another story leaks through it.
The air here folds like paper. Something on the other side is pressing to get in.
A rift. Stitch it, ward it or let it go. All three are fine.
echo: An echo of a rift somewhere else, a flicker on the page.
It isn’t really here. It’s a reflection of trouble further off.
An echo. Follow it, and it leads to the real thing.
stitch: The seam, where the two stories meet. A thread through here would close it.
The edges of the tear, waiting for a needle.
This is where it all comes apart, and where it all goes back together.
exit: The way out, back to the Hushlands. It smells of your own weather.
A door of ordinary light. Home is on the other side of it.
The way you came in. It stays open for as long as you need it.

sleeping: A chest from another story, locked with somebody else’s idea of a lock.
It sits in the corner as if it’s been waiting for this chapter.
Heavy, carved and mostly honest. Probably.
opened: Open, and empty but for a smell of another story’s weather.
Already opened. Its lid rests against the wall, satisfied.
Nothing left but a few loose threads from the page it came from.

curio: A curio from the story next door. It hums when you hold it near the light.
Something odd and small, left here on purpose or by a very tidy accident.
A curio. Oriel would want to catalogue it. Brannoch would want to know what it’s for.
nook: A hearth-nook: a warm hollow in the wall, with a small fire that belongs to nobody’s story.
Somebody left a kettle here, and it’s already warm. Rest a while, once.
A quiet corner the rift forgot to fill. The whole Company can sit here and catch their breath.

sleeping: A sleeping lantern. Light it, and every lantern you’ve lit will know.
Soot on the glass and a wick that’s waited three hundred years. It won’t mind another minute.
Cold for now. Once it’s lit, the Company can sit beside it and catch their breath.
lit: Lit and steady. If everyone ever goes offline, they’ll wake at the last lantern they rested at.
A lit lantern on the old road. Sit here a while and the whole Company rests.
Its light reaches just far enough to feel like somewhere.

spring: New leaves, still crumpled from the bud. The tree looks pleased with itself.
Blossom on the lower branches, and a blackbird working out a tune.
Sap rising. You can almost hear it, if you lean close.
summer: Full leaf and deep shade underneath. A good tree to sit against.
Bees in the canopy and a cool patch at the roots.
The leaves rustle like a crowd settling in before a story.
autumn: Leaves the colour of Tamsin’s scarf, letting go one at a time.
Half bare, half gold, and taking its time about the rest.
A crunch underfoot and a smell of woodsmoke from somewhere.
winter: Bare branches, and a hat of snow on the highest fork.
Asleep for the winter. It’ll wake when it’s ready.
Frost on every twig, as if it’s been sketched in silver.

pine: A tall pine, dropping needles on everything with great patience.
It smells sharp and green. The owls like the straight ones best.
Resin on the bark, sticky and bright. The whole wood smells of it.
birch: Pale bark, good kindling, terrible hiding spot.
A birch, its bark peeling in thin curls you could almost write on.
Slim and white. It catches the light before anything else does.
rock: A good sitting rock, warm on the sunny side.
A rock. It was here first, and it knows it.
Lichen in three colours, slowly arguing over the top.
bush: Sweet in autumn, sour in spring, nosy all year.
Leaves, twigs and a small rustle that stops when you stop.
A low bush. Something has made a very comfortable den underneath.

day: A clear sky, the kind that makes the road look shorter.
Not a cloud. The wind has somewhere else to be today.
Blue from edge to edge. A good day for finishing something small.
night: Stars from edge to edge. Milo names a few, mostly wrongly.
A clear night. Somewhere far to the west, the Great Lighthouse is turning.
The sky’s so clear you could count the stars. Oriel has, twice.
dawn: Dawn, pale at the edges. The birds are arguing about who woke first.
The sky is going gold from the bottom up.
First light. The lanterns look almost shy of it.
dusk: Dusk, and the sky goes the colour of hearthberries.
The light goes amber and long, and every shadow gets ideas.
Evening coming on. Time to think about the kettle.

day: Rain, steady and soft. The kind that makes the tent smell wonderful.
Grey rain on everything. The birches look pleased to have a wash.
It’s raining, so the whole world is quieter. Milo turns his collar up.
night: Rain in the dark, drumming on the canvas like a patient friend.
Night rain. The lanterns wear little haloes.
It’s raining softly. A good night to be near a fire.
dawn: A wet dawn. The birds are singing anyway, only a little quieter.
Early rain on the tent roof, soft as someone tapping to see if you’re up.
The light comes up grey and gentle, and the puddles catch it first.
dusk: Rain at dusk, and the lanterns come on one by one along the road.
The evening rain has settled in for the night. The kettle agrees with it.
Dusk and drizzle. The road shines like it’s been polished for someone.

day: Snow, falling slowly enough to follow one flake all the way down.
Everything’s gone white and hushed. Your footprints are the only news.
Snow on the stumps, snow on the bench, snow on Milo’s hood.
night: Snow at night, blue in the lantern-light.
The snow’s still falling. By morning the road will be new.
Quiet snow. Even the owls have stopped to watch it.
dawn: Snow at dawn, pink at the edges where the sun is trying.
First light on new snow. Nobody has walked anywhere yet, so every path is yours.
The morning’s so still you can hear the snow settling.
dusk: Snow in the dusk, going blue as the light goes.
Evening snow. The lanterns make little rooms of light in it.
The flakes come slower as the day ends, as if they’re tired too.

day: Mist in the hollows, lifting like a curtain nobody’s in a hurry to raise.
The far trees have gone soft and grey. The near ones pretend not to notice.
A white day. Sounds carry strangely, and a crow laughs from nowhere.
night: Night mist, and the lanterns glow in it like peaches.
Mist in the dark. Something in the pines hoots, then thinks better of it.
You can’t see far tonight. The camp feels closer for it.
dawn: Dawn mist over everything. The sun is somewhere behind it, taking its time.
Mist beaded on every blade of grass. Walk through it and your boots come out shining.
The world’s still being drawn this morning. Only the near things are finished.
dusk: Dusk mist rolling in from the low ground, taking the far trees first.
The evening’s gone soft and grey at the edges. The lanterns make it cosy.
Mist and dusk together. The fire sounds closer than it is.

day: A good wind, tugging at scarves and hats. Milo holds on to his.
The grass runs ahead of the wind, the way it does.
Wind in the trees, all of them talking at once.
night: Wind in the dark, rattling the tent pegs to see if they’re awake.
A blustery night. The fire leans one way, then thinks better of it.
The wind’s up. Every lantern on the road is flickering, and holding.
dawn: A windy dawn. The clouds are in a hurry, and the sun keeps peeking between them.
Morning wind, cold and clean, blowing the night off the hills.
The wind got up before anyone else and has been busy with the washing.
dusk: Wind at dusk, pushing the last of the light over the hills.
A gusty evening. The fire crackles as if it’s trying to keep up with the talk.
The wind’s turning cold with the evening. Scarves on.

day: Leaves on the wind, gold and red, going wherever it’s going.
A leaf lands on Milo’s hood. He leaves it there.
The ground is crunchy and bright. Autumn has arrived all at once.
night: Leaves skittering along in the dark, on some errand of their own.
Autumn at night: the rustle of leaves you can hear but not see.
A leaf taps at the lantern glass, then blows on.
dawn: Dawn, and the leaves that fell overnight are all over the path, gold and damp.
Morning light through thinning branches. More leaves down than yesterday.
Early leaves spinning in the first light, as if they’re not ready to land.
dusk: Leaves spinning down in the last of the light.
The evening is full of falling leaves and woodsmoke.
A long gold dusk, and the trees letting go a little at a time.

sleeping: The Last Bridge, Brannoch’s work. Its far end is still in the Hush, and it won’t take anyone across till the wood wakes.
Level as a table and humming a low note. The deck waits for the Whisperwood to wake before it takes anyone across.
A Cinderfolk bridge with its far side in the Hush. It’ll take you over when the wood wakes, and not a day before.
opened: The Last Bridge, Brannoch’s work, over a stream that ran dry long ago. The road goes over it and on into the wood.
A Cinderfolk footbridge with no water under it. It hums a low note when Milo walks over it on the road north.
Its stream is long gone, but the bridge kept its post. The road runs across it, and the Whisperwood sleeps beyond.

hooklight: Lit from the Hook. The big one stays home, so home stays safe.
riddle-note: A folded note in Tamsin’s round hand, the ink gone brown. It starts with a riddle, naturally.
Birch-bark paper, folded small. Someone meant for this to be found, and puzzled over.
One of Tamsin’s Riddle Notes. The Tollkeeper keeps the rest, and he’s very particular about them.

read: The Scribe reads the glyphs aloud: a builder’s note, asking whoever comes next to finish the stair.
“It’s a list,” the Scribe says, tracing the carving. “Stones, lintels, and one line that just says ‘lunch’.”
The Scribe finds a Maker’s mark and a date. “Older than the road,” she says, “and still level.”
The Scribe reads the plinth: “Unfinished, as requested.” Someone has added, smaller, “She was right.”
The letters are worn nearly smooth. The Scribe makes out Tamsin’s name, and a line about a ribbon left untied.
“There’s more on the back,” the Scribe says. “It just says ‘Wait for the next one.’ In her hand, I think.”
